title: Fed expected to hold rates steady Oct. 28, days before the midterms
excerpt: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady on Oct. 28, less than a week before midterm elections centered on the cost of living, Reuters reported.
content:
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady on Wednesday, Oct. 28, less than a week before midterm elections in which the cost of living is a central issue, Reuters reported.

The Federal Open Market Committee met Oct. 27-28, with its decision scheduled for 2 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday, followed by a press conference from Chair Kevin Warsh at 2:30 p.m., according to Reuters and the Fed calendar summarized in previews of the meeting.

Holding rates would leave the federal funds target range at 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent, where it has stood since a quarter-point increase in September. In a Reuters poll conducted Oct. 16-20, 94 of 100 economists expected the Fed to hold rates at this meeting, and all 100 anticipated an increase in December, Reuters reported. CME Group's FedWatch tool put the probability of a hold at about 90 percent.

Why a pause, and why it may not last

Officials had signaled the central bank could be patient after last month's increase, Reuters reported, while it waits to see whether inflation moderates or stays strong enough to warrant more hikes. Consumer price inflation was 3.7 percent over the 12 months to September, above the Fed's 2 percent longer-run objective, according to previews citing Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

The forces pushing prices up, as described by economists and policymakers in the Reuters report, include the lingering energy cost shock and tariff effects, strong demand from the artificial intelligence industry, and healthy consumer spending. That mix is why a hold this week is widely read as a pause rather than a pivot: markets still see further increases as likely before year end.

What it means for readers here

The Fed's benchmark rate does not set any single household's loan rate directly, but it influences borrowing costs across the economy, including mortgages, auto loans, credit cards and business credit. For Webb County families and small businesses weighing a large purchase or a loan, the practical question after Wednesday is not only what the Fed did, but what Warsh signals about December.

A hold that comes with hawkish language, warning that more increases may be needed, can still push bond yields and borrowing costs higher. A hold with a softer tone could do the opposite. The statement and the press conference, not the headline decision alone, will carry that signal.

The decision also lands days before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republican Party retains control of Congress, Reuters noted. Holding rates this week moves the rate discussion past the election itself, but it does not remove the cost-of-living debate from the campaign.
